context: Zoomable treemap of a synthetic file system with 471 files across 8 top-level directories, 3 depth levels (dirs → subdirs → files), 8 categorical colors from a Tol colorblind-safe palette, and click-to-zoom interaction with 750ms transitions and breadcrumb navigation.
first_impression: Dense but organized — the color grouping immediately conveys the 8-directory structure, though the root view renders all three levels simultaneously, producing a lot of small, barely-readable leaf cells.
what_works: The Tol palette with lightness modulation by depth (dark for depth-1, mid for depth-2, light for leaves) encodes hierarchy without adding more hues, keeping color overload in check despite 8 categories. The zoom interaction plus breadcrumb trail effectively offloads cognitive work — drilling into a directory collapses everything else, making the per-level views genuinely readable.
what_doesnt: At the root view, hundreds of leaf-level file cells are visible simultaneously alongside their parent subdirs and grandparent dirs, which competes for attention and makes the density feel overwhelming before the user discovers the zoom interaction. Label suppression helps but many visible cells still show truncated or invisible text, reducing the information value of the root-level overview.
